title: Intarsia colourwork: introduction
sourceNotes: Intarsia technique is widely described in Mary Thomas, Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). Out of copyright UK/EU. Modern bobbin management and twist-direction guidance is standard craft practice; no single PD attribution. sourceType: SYNTHESISED.

glossaryTerms.definition: A colourwork technique in which each colour block uses its own separate length of yarn, twisted at boundaries to prevent holes. The fabric remains single-thickness regardless of colour count.
A colourwork technique in which all colours are carried across every row, weaving in the non-working yarn at intervals at the back to form a double-thickness fabric with floats.

content.text: In
intarsia
, each colour block has its own ball of yarn. At every colour change, you twist the two yarns around each other once. This locks the blocks together and stops holes forming at the joins. Unlike
Fair Isle
, there are no floats across the back. Each colour only travels across the stitches it covers, so the fabric stays a single layer.

You need two or more yarn colours, needles, and a supply of small bobbins or yarn butterflies (small hand-wound lengths). Intarsia is worked flat rather than in the round; knitting a motif in the round is possible but requires an adapted technique.
Step by step
Wind each colour into a small bobbin or butterfly of yarn. Long lengths tangle; 1 to 2 metres per colour section is practical for most motifs.
Work across the row in the background colour until you reach the first colour-change boundary.
Before picking up the new colour, wrap the old colour yarn anticlockwise once around the new colour yarn. This twist links the two sections. Drop the old colour; pick up the new.
Continue knitting in the new colour across its stitch block.
At each subsequent colour boundary, repeat the twist: the yarn currently in use wraps once around the incoming colour before being dropped.
On wrong-side rows, the twist direction reverses so the wraps sit on the wrong side of the fabric. On a wrong-side row, bring the old colour up and to the left over the new colour before dropping it.
At the end of the piece, weave in each yarn end separately. Run it along the colour boundary on the wrong side. Do not weave it across the back of the next colour block.
Where you'll see it

Intarsia appears in flat knitting with large blocks of colour: geometric shapes, picture knitting (animals, letters, seasonal motifs), and the bold colour blocks found in 1960s and 70s knitwear. It keeps the fabric single-thickness. For large motif areas or non-elastic fibres like cotton, intarsia is a better choice than stranded colourwork. Stranding adds thickness and can cause uneven tension.
Common faults

Holes at colour boundaries. The most common problem: the two yarns were not twisted at the boundary. Check that the outgoing colour wrapped over the incoming colour before being dropped, on every row including wrong-side rows.

Tangled bobbins. Intarsia with more than 4 or 5 colour sections requires careful bobbin management. Work from left to right across the bobbins, untwisting after every second row by lifting the work and letting the bobbins dangle free.

Loose stitch at the first stitch after each colour join. The tension at a join is typically looser than in the middle of a colour block. Pulling the new colour slightly tighter on the first stitch after a join, then normalising on the second stitch, helps this.

What to try next: work a simple two-colour motif using an intarsia chart. A small heart or diamond, 15 to 20 stitches wide, is a good starting point. The regular shape lets you practise the joins before moving on to larger or more complex motifs.
